questions.q: What does T1, the energy relaxation time, physically measure?
options: The average time for a qubit prepared in |1> to decay back down to |0>, losing energy to its environment
The average time for a qubit to be fabricated on the chip
The time it takes to cool the dilution refrigerator to base temperature
The frequency at which microwave control pulses are sent to the qubit
questions.explain: T1 is specifically about energy loss -- how long, on average, an excited qubit holds its energy before relaxing to the ground state. It's also called amplitude damping.

questions.q: How does T2 (dephasing time) differ from T1 (energy relaxation time)?
options: T2 measures how long a superposition keeps its phase relationship intact, which can be lost even without any energy loss, whereas T1 specifically measures energy loss
T2 and T1 measure exactly the same physical process and are always numerically identical
T2 only applies to qubits that have never been read out
T2 measures the physical temperature of the dilution refrigerator
questions.explain: Dephasing (T2) can scramble a superposition's phase relationship without the qubit losing any energy at all, which is a distinct physical process from the energy relaxation that T1 captures.

questions.q: According to the relationship 1/T2 = 1/(2*T1) + 1/T_phi, why can T2 never exceed 2*T1?
options: Because 1/T_phi is always zero or positive, so 1/T2 is always at least 1/(2*T1), meaning T2 is always at most 2*T1, with equality only when pure dephasing is negligible
Because T1 and T2 are defined to always be exactly equal by convention
Because T_phi is always negative, which forces T2 above 2*T1
There is no such relationship -- T2 can exceed 2*T1 in real devices
questions.explain: Since the pure dephasing contribution 1/T_phi can only add to 1/(2*T1) (never subtract), T2 is mathematically capped at 2*T1, reaching that ceiling only in the idealized limit of negligible pure dephasing.

questions.q: For a qubit with T1 = 100 microseconds and a pure dephasing time T_phi = 100 microseconds, what does the relationship 1/T2 = 1/(2*T1) + 1/T_phi give for T2?
options: Approximately 66.7 microseconds, well under the 200-microsecond ceiling of 2*T1
Exactly 200 microseconds, the maximum possible value
Exactly 100 microseconds, equal to T1
Approximately 300 microseconds, exceeding 2*T1
questions.explain: Plugging in: 1/T2 = 1/200 + 1/100 = 0.015, so T2 = 1/0.015 ~= 66.7 microseconds -- comfortably below the 2*T1 = 200 microsecond bound, as it must be.

questions.q: Why does coherence time place a practical ceiling on circuit depth in a quantum computation?
options: Because every gate and idle period takes time during which the qubit is decaying and dephasing, so once total run time becomes a significant fraction of T1 or T2, the result becomes unreliable
Because circuit depth is defined as the number of qubits on the chip, which has nothing to do with T1 or T2
Because longer circuits always run on a different, unrelated piece of hardware
Because T1 and T2 only matter during qubit fabrication, not during computation
questions.explain: A quantum circuit accumulates risk of decoherence throughout its entire run time -- the more sequential gate layers (depth), the more total time elapses, and the higher the chance decay or dephasing corrupts the result before it can be measured.
